Notes from the review, circulated to the whole set. Thanks to everyone who made time for it.

The first thing to say is that the fresh procedure is clear enough, and the consequence is a large improvement over the method we used last quarter. We can present that the count of failures has dropped, and the result is simple to clarify: we confirm every modify before it lands, and we invariably check the build after it. That is the whole idea, and it seems to work.

There is still a difficulty, however, and it is important. The way we keep records of each release is quite strange. Many of the notes are hidden in places nobody can find, and a person joining the team would find it very hard to obtain a real picture of what happened. We should therefore build a easy index, keep it near the release notes, and use it to give every reader a clear place to begin.

The next problem concerns time. Reviews often take about a week, because we ask for changes and then wait. Maybe we can reduce that. One idea is to choose a smaller group of reviewers for small changes, and to allow the whole team to help only on the big ones. Another is to remove the second sign-off entirely for anything under a small threshold. Both would make the process faster, though neither is free.

I also think we should show the numbers more often. If the result of each release is displayed in one place, and the number of open problems is always visible, people can find the trouble spots without asking. That is a small change and it provides a great deal.

Last thing. The old tooling is still in use in a few places, and it is a real risk. We should change the remaining scripts, check them, and then remove the old ones. It is not difficult work, but it is easy to keep putting it off, and the result of leaving it is that the subsequent person has to do it beneath pressure.

Please tell me if any portion of this seems wrong. I will finish the write-up following the subsequent review, and I would very much like to validate the plan before then.

A second note, since the first was already long. The important item is that we start, not that we complete quickly. If we start little and display the outcome regularly, the complication stops being odd and becomes ordinary work. That is usually how these changes go.

We should additionally describe the technique to the wider group. A short memo helps: what changed, why it is crucial, and what people should validate before they build. If the memo is evident, the number of questions drops, and the upshot is that we decrease the moment spent on help rather than increase it.

The final idea is a small one. We often excise old scripts and then find that some hidden dependency is still using them. A fast verify before we excise anything would assist. It is a small change, but the consequence of skipping it is a strange failure late in the release, and those are always hard to describe.

I believe we should select two of these and finalise them this quarter, rather than begin all four and finalise none. The typical result of a sizable list is that the essential items are the ones we never reach. So: select the modest ones, show the upshot, and let the group assist with the rest.

If any of this seems wrong, tell me. It is easier to modify the method now than after we build the thing. I would rather we check the idea early, check what we can, and then begin.

One more small thing, and then I will stop. The build often fails for a strange reason that turns out to be a small change nobody thought was important. If we show the whole result of each check, rather than the last line, the problem is usually easy to find. It is a very quick change and it would help a great deal.
